To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

proteins can be labeled by incubation with [35S]-methionine and -cysteine without the presence of living cells, that the labeling is resistant to dissociation under conditions that disrupt covalent bonds, that the labeling effect is more efficient with [ 35 S]-cysteine, and that the label is not consistently associated with individual amino acids.
incubation of [35]methionine or [35]cysteinewith proteins resulted in incorporation of 35S radioactivity into the protein that was resistant to dissociating agents.
proteins spontaneously label with [35S]-cysteine and [35]S-methionine in vitro.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the study of protein function.
the spontaneous labeling of proteins by 35S-containing amino acids in vitro and the effect of this labeling on subsequent metabolic studies.
the identification of proteins involved in the pathophysiology of the acute respiratory distress syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the labeling of proteins with [ 35S ]methionine and/ or [ 35S]cys- teine in the absence of cells is not an artifact but rather is a spontaneous reaction that can occur with a variety of proteins and that can be used as a labeling method for proteins.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the labeling of protein by [35S] methionine and [ 35S] cysteine is not due to the presence of the sulfur-containing amino acids, but rather is an artifact of the labeling procedure.
[35S]labeling of proteins can be achieved in vitro in the absence of living cells.

the labeling of proteins with [ 35 S]methionine or cysteine in the presence of bovine serum albumin, globulins, catalase, human globulin, or hemoglobin results in the incorporation of the  35 S label into the protein, which is resistant to dissociation, dilution, and TCA precipitation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the labeling of proteins with [ 35 S]cysteines or [ 35 S ]methionines in the absence of cellular components can be a powerful tool in the study of protein function.
[35S] methionine and [ 35S] cysteine can spontaneously incorporate into proteins in the absence cells and that this labeling can be stable and resistant to various conditions.
the use of [35S]-methionine and cystein to label protein is not as specific as once thought.
